::: {.callout-note}
## A note on how this was made

Built by directing an AI research assistant: I set the research question, cohort rules, and interpretation; Claude wrote and ran the code, including the API pull. Data comes from the public [ClinicalTrials.gov API v2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/data-api/api) (no key required); the fetch script ships with this post.
:::

## The question

Clinical trial planning runs on duration assumptions. Enrollment forecasts, budgets, and site strategies all start from "how long will this take?" — so before building anything fancier, it's worth asking what the public registry can tell us about the drivers of trial duration using nothing but information available **at trial launch**: phase, planned size, site footprint, and who's running it.

This is the first post in a planned series working toward enrollment forecasting and site selection. The goal here is deliberately modest: establish the dataset, map the univariate patterns, fit a baseline regression, and be honest about what study-level registry data can and can't support.

## Data

The pull: 12,000 **completed, interventional Phase 2 and Phase 3** trials from ClinicalTrials.gov, flattened to one row per study — phase, actual enrollment, start and primary-completion dates, lead sponsor class, and site/country counts. Duration is start → primary completion, in months.



One filter matters more than all the others, so it gets its own paragraph. **Restricting to completed trials creates survivorship bias against recent cohorts**: a trial that started in 2023 can only appear in a completed-trials dataset if it finished fast. Left unhandled, this makes recent trials look artificially quick and contaminates every other coefficient. The fix here is blunt but effective: keep trials that **started 2000–2018**, so even slow trials (up to ~7 years) had time to complete before the data was pulled. The right long-term fix is survival analysis with ongoing trials included as censored observations — that's on the roadmap, not in this post.

## What moves duration — and what doesn't

::: {#cell-fig-univariate .cell execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Duration distributions. Left: by phase — the differences are small. Right: by sponsor type — the differences are not.](index_files/figure-html/fig-univariate-output-1.png){#fig-univariate width=1817 height=692}
:::
:::


::: {#tbl-medians .cell tbl-cap='Median duration (months) by phase and sponsor type.' execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown}
| phase     |   Industry |   Academic / other |   Government / network |
|:----------|-----------:|-------------------:|-----------------------:|
| Phase 1/2 |       28.1 |                 35 |                     36 |
| Phase 2   |       17.6 |                 39 |                     42 |
| Phase 2/3 |       20   |                 29 |                     40 |
| Phase 3   |       20   |                 37 |                     51 |
:::
:::


Two things the table makes hard to ignore:

**Phase is a weak predictor.** Phase 3 trials — larger, multi-country, more expensive — complete their primary endpoint *no slower* than Phase 2 trials in the same sponsor column. Whatever intuition says about big confirmatory trials grinding on for years, the median Phase 3 is comparable to the median Phase 2. Scale apparently buys operational muscle in proportion to its ambitions.

**Sponsor type is a strong one.** Industry trials run roughly **half the duration** of government/network trials in every phase. Some of that is real operational difference (dedicated CROs, recruitment budgets, site payments), and some is that different sponsors run structurally different studies — endpoint choice, population rarity, follow-up length. Registry-level data can't fully separate those, and this post won't pretend it can.

::: {#cell-fig-confounding .cell execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Enrollment vs. duration, colored by sponsor. The raw relationship between size and duration is nearly flat — because bigger trials are disproportionately industry trials, which are faster.](index_files/figure-html/fig-confounding-output-1.png){#fig-confounding width=1152 height=698}
:::
:::


This chart is the reason the regression below exists. Pooled, enrollment looks unrelated to duration — trials with 500+ participants finish as fast as 50-participant trials. Split by sponsor, an upward slope reappears *within* each group. Classic confounding: **who** runs big trials masks what big trials cost in time. The regression will push this one step further — and find that even the within-sponsor slope isn't really about patient counts.

## A baseline model

OLS on log duration, with the launch-time features and start-year fixed effects. Nothing exotic — the point is to measure how much these features explain together, and to get the enrollment effect conditional on sponsor.



::: {#cell-fig-coefs .cell execution_count=8}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Coefficients on log duration with 95% CIs (start-year fixed effects not shown). Exponentiate to read as multiplicative effects.](index_files/figure-html/fig-coefs-output-1.png){#fig-coefs width=1190 height=662}
:::
:::


::: {#cell-model-summary .cell execution_count=9}

::: {#model-summary .cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown}

Reading the fit:

- **Sponsor dominates.** Holding phase, size, sites, and vintage fixed, a government/network-sponsored
  trial runs about **2.3×** the duration of an industry trial. Academic sponsors sit in between.
- **The time cost of scale lives in the footprint, not the head-count.** With only sponsor and phase
  controlled, enrollment has a modest positive elasticity (0.09 — doubling enrollment adds
  ~6%). Add the footprint variables and it collapses to 0.01,
  while **sites** (0.14 per log-unit) and **multi-country operation** (+23%)
  pick up the effect. Conditional on how widely a trial is spread, more patients barely cost time;
  spreading the trial wider does. For planning, that inverts the usual intuition: the enrollment
  target matters less than the operational structure chosen to hit it.
- **Phase remains a modest effect** — Phase 3 is only slightly longer than Phase 2, all else equal.
- **R² = 0.24.** Launch-time registry features explain a real but minor share of duration
  variance. Most of what determines trial length — therapeutic area, endpoint follow-up length,
  protocol complexity, site quality — isn't in these columns yet. That's the roadmap, not a failure:
  a planning model needs to know how much the cheap features buy before paying for expensive ones.

:::
:::


## Caveats

- **Primary completion ≠ done.** Duration here ends at the primary endpoint's completion date; full study close-out takes longer.
- **Registry hygiene varies.** Location lists are incomplete for older trials (site counts are floors, not truths), and `ACTUAL` enrollment is self-reported.
- **Completed-only + 2000–2018 window** removes the worst survivorship bias but also drops terminated trials — the model predicts duration *conditional on finishing*, which is the optimistic version of the planning question.
- **No therapeutic area yet.** Oncology and vaccines have famously different tempos; condition text needs mapping to areas before it can enter the model.

## Where this series goes next

1. **Add therapeutic area** (map conditions → MeSH-style categories) — the strongest known predictor left on the table.
2. **Survival framing**: include ongoing and terminated trials as censored/competing observations instead of filtering to completed ones.
3. **Enrollment-rate modeling** — participants per site per month, the quantity trial planners actually forecast — using the AACT flat files, which carry richer design fields than the v2 API pull.
4. **Site selection**: which countries and site footprints historically hit planned enrollment, framed as a ranking problem.

---

*Data: [ClinicalTrials.gov API v2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/data-api/api), pulled July 2026 — 12,000 completed interventional Phase 2/3 studies; analysis cohort restricted to 2000–2018 starts. Fetch script: `fetch_aact_sample.py` alongside this post.*
